title: State of Our Unions 2026: The Dating Recession | Institute for Family Studies
gist: The 2025 National Dating Landscape Survey of 5,275 unmarried 22-35 year olds finds a 'dating recession': only ~30% are currently dating and just 31% date monthly or more, despite 51% wanting a relationship and 86% expecting to marry. The binding constraints are money (52% cite it as the top barrier), low dating efficacy (only ~1 in 3 trust their dating skills) and breakup scarring (55% more reluctant after a breakup) — not fear of commitment, which only 18% endorse.

insights.claim: Only about 30% of unmarried U.S. young adults aged 22-35 report currently dating either casually or exclusively, per the 2025 National Dating Landscape Survey of 5,275 respondents.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The addressable market for dating apps, wedding services and household formation is shrinking at the top of the funnel, not just at the marriage stage.
insights.quote: Only about 30% of young adults reported that they are dating, either casually or exclusively.
insights.locator: Only About 1 in 3 of Young Adults is Actively Dating

insights.claim: Only 31% of young adults are 'active daters' who date once a month or more — 26% of women versus 36% of men — while 74% of women and 64% of men dated not at all or only a few times in the past year.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Dating-adjacent consumer spend (restaurants, bars, events, apps) is being drained by a behavioural, not preference-driven, collapse.
insights.quote: Nearly three-quarters of women (74%) and nearly two-thirds of men (64%) in our survey reported they had not dated or dated only a few times in the last year.
insights.locator: Only About 1 in 3 of Young Adults is Actively Dating

insights.claim: The gap between desire and behaviour is the core anomaly: 51% of unmarried young adults say they are single but interested in starting a relationship, yet only ~30% are actually dating.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Demand exists but is not clearing — the bottleneck is matching and skills infrastructure, a product opportunity rather than a preference shift.
insights.locator: However, at the time of the survey, only about 30%

insights.claim: Interest in starting a relationship is far higher among men (60%) than women (47%), while only about one in six of either sex says they are single and uninterested.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A gender imbalance in expressed demand implies persistent skew on the supply side of dating platforms and unequal pricing power in the match market.
insights.locator: About half (51%) of our respondents reported they were single

insights.claim: Satisfaction with dating options is low and largely disconnected from behaviour: only 21% are satisfied with their options, 39% dissatisfied, yet dating frequency and satisfaction correlate only weakly (r = .16).
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Improving match quality alone is unlikely to restart dating volume — the binding constraint sits elsewhere.
insights.quote: Only 21% reported they were satisfied with their options.
insights.locator: The frequency of dating could be related to their satisfaction

insights.claim: Young adults who say they do not expect to marry (14% of the sample) report the same low level of active dating as those who do expect to marry, suggesting the dating slowdown is not driven by marital intent.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Cuts against the theory that falling marriage aspiration explains the dating slump; the cause is structural to dating itself.
insights.locator: Interestingly, respondents in our survey who did not expect to marry

insights.claim: Only about one in three young adults expresses much faith in their own dating skills, a construct the authors label 'dating efficacy.'
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Reframes the dating slump as a human-capital deficit — a trainable skill gap — which implies a services market rather than a matching-algorithm market.
insights.locator: Overall, we found that dating efficacy was low

insights.claim: Only about a quarter of young adults feel confident approaching someone they are romantically interested in (29% of men, 21% of women), the most basic initiating skill in dating.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Approach anxiety is the single narrowest choke point; products that remove or substitute for the approach step capture the most value.
insights.locator: Only a quarter expressed

insights.claim: Only 37% of young adults trust their own judgment in choosing a dating partner, 34% are confident discussing feelings with a partner, and 36% feel able to read social cues on dates.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Deficits are in interpretation and communication, not access — areas where coaching and AI assistants could plausibly intervene.
insights.locator: A little over a third (37%) said they trusted their judgment

insights.claim: Dating efficacy correlates positively with dating frequency at r = .26, a small-to-medium effect that makes skills a plausible causal lever on dating behaviour.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Quantifies the upside of skills intervention: real but modest, so expect incremental rather than step-change effects.
insights.locator: There was a small-to-medium, positive correlation between dating efficacy

insights.claim: Only 38% of young adults are confident they are attractive to potential dating partners, with almost no gender gap (39% of men, 37% of women).
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Self-perceived desirability, not objective market access, is a widespread drag — relevant to the appearance, fitness and cosmetic categories.
insights.locator: Thirty-eight percent were confident that they were attractive

insights.claim: Only 28% of young adults say they can stay positive after a bad date or relationship setback, making low resilience — not low desire — the defining feature of the modern dating market.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Emotional scarring is a durable dampener: expect dating activity to stay depressed even if match supply improves.
insights.locator: In addition, only about a quarter (28%) reported being able to stay positive

insights.claim: More than half (55%) of young adults agree their breakups have made them more reluctant to begin new romantic relationships, and 45% say they have passed up new romantic opportunities because of past bad experiences.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A self-reinforcing withdrawal loop — each failed relationship removes participants from the pool, compounding the recession.
insights.locator: More than half (55%) agreed that their breakups have made them

insights.claim: Over a third (36%) of young adults admit they now end relationships too quickly to avoid the pain of a bad breakup, an avoidance behaviour that shortens relationship duration independent of match quality.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Explains high churn in relationships and in dating apps: users exit early by design, driving repeat subscription cycles but low satisfaction.
insights.locator: Also, more than a third (36%) agreed that they now end relationships

insights.claim: Breakups are not uniformly negative in this data: 63% say their breakups were necessary and facilitated personal growth and 67% say they are now better at ending relationships that do not meet their needs.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The scarring narrative is partial — a majority extracts learning, meaning interventions should target the scarred minority-to-half, not everyone.
insights.locator: On the positive side, many agreed their relationship breakups were necessary

insights.claim: Breakup scarring compounds an already documented mental-health crisis in this generation, so dating withdrawal should be read as a recovery response rather than as apathy.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Links the dating recession to the broader youth mental-health trade — therapy platforms, SSRIs, and social-media regulation all touch the same cohort.
insights.locator: And this comes on top of this generation’s well-documented mental-health challenges

themes.theme: Money as the Number One Dating Barrier

insights.claim: The single biggest self-reported barrier to dating is not having enough money, cited by 52% of young adults — 58% of men and 46% of women — ahead of every social or emotional factor.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Dating volume is directly exposed to youth real incomes; a cost-of-living squeeze mechanically suppresses family formation and, downstream, births.
insights.locator: Interestingly, the biggest barrier to dating they expressed was not enough money

insights.claim: Money is a barrier in a current-tangible sense — affording the actual dates — not just a future-abstract threshold for marriage readiness.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Distinguishes two separate financial channels; the near-term one responds to cheap-date substitutes and discretionary-income swings, not to wealth accumulation.
insights.quote: Dating for contemporary young adults has a price tag, and they feel the pinch.
insights.locator: Money concerns are not just future-abstract

insights.claim: Nearly 75% of young adults agree that money and finances are a major barrier to getting married, with the belief strongest among 22-29 year olds.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Housing, tuition and employment costs are transmitted directly into marriage-rate suppression — a policy-sensitive channel.
insights.locator: For instance, nearly 75% of our respondents agreed

insights.claim: Because contemporary dating is organised around commercial activities, the culture itself has priced out participants — a redefinition of a 'date' away from restaurant-and-concert spending would expand the market.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Bearish for the premium-experience share of youth discretionary spend, bullish for low-cost social formats and third places.
insights.locator: Maybe they can help shift the general dating culture

insights.claim: Lack of confidence (49%) and bad past dating experiences (48%) are the two largest non-financial barriers, with past bad experience the single most cited barrier among women (50%).
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Emotional and financial constraints are comparable in magnitude — any fix must address both, not just affordability.
insights.locator: At the top of this list were lack of confidence (49%)

insights.claim: Contrary to the standard cultural narrative, fear of commitment barely registers: only 18% cite not wanting to commit long-term and only 27% cite losing personal freedom as dating barriers.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Invalidates the 'young people don't want relationships' thesis underlying much commentary on falling marriage rates — the constraint is capability, not preference.
insights.locator: Although there is a common notion that young adults want to avoid

insights.claim: Young adults strongly endorse traditional, relationship-building purposes for dating — forming serious relationships (83% of women, 74% of men) and creating emotional connections (83% of women, 76% of men) — over casual or social ones.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Product and cultural bets premised on a permanent hookup culture are misreading revealed preference; the demand is for commitment-oriented formats.
insights.locator: Young Adults Desire a Dating Culture Aimed at Forming Serious Relationships

insights.claim: Explicitly social purposes for dating rank far lower than relational ones: fitting in with others (17%), gaining social validation (16%) and being part of social activities (24%).
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Status-driven dating is a minority motivation; gamified, social-proof-heavy app design is misaligned with what the majority say they want.
insights.locator: such as fitting in with others (17%)

insights.claim: Physical intimacy is endorsed as a dating purpose by 45% overall and produces by far the largest gender gap in the survey — 55% of men versus 35% of women.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The one genuinely large gender divergence in the dataset; a persistent source of mismatched expectations that dating products must arbitrate.
insights.locator: Engaging in physical intimacy (45%) was also endorsed

insights.claim: Outside of physical intimacy, dating experiences and challenges are remarkably similar for women and men, so interventions do not need to be gender-differentiated.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Undercuts the gender-war framing of the dating crisis; suggests a single unified product rather than segmented male/female offerings.
insights.locator: Note that dating education for young adults will not need to differentiate

insights.claim: Regardless of a respondent's current age, the gap between now and the age they expect to marry stays constant at about 5-6 years, meaning the marital horizon slides upward rather than shrinking with time.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A structural reason marriage keeps being deferred: expectations are anchored to a rolling horizon, so cohort marriage rates will keep undershooting stated intentions.
insights.quote: the age they expect to marry is not fixed: it appears to slide upward as they get older rather than shrink with the passage of time
insights.locator: regardless of current age, respondents’ marital horizon

insights.claim: Median expected age of marriage is 33 for women and almost 35 for men, and among the oldest respondents (33-35) it rises to about 39 for both sexes.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Expected marriage ages well above the current mean at first marriage imply further deferral — bearish for near-term fertility and household formation.
insights.locator: The overall median age of expected marriage was 33 for women

insights.claim: Only 30% of young adults believe there is an ideal age to marry at all, and among those who do the modal answer is 30 — uncorrelated with religiosity or spirituality.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Normative timing pressure has largely dissolved, removing a traditional forcing mechanism for marriage decisions.
insights.locator: Only 30% said yes, there is an ideal age to marry.

insights.claim: Marital salience averages just 3.3 on a 6-point scale and does not differ by age group, so the personal importance of marriage is static across the 22-35 window rather than rising with age.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: No natural urgency ramp exists — marketers and policymakers cannot rely on age itself to convert intent into action.
insights.locator: The average rating was 3.3 (on a 6-point scale)

insights.claim: Despite the modest average salience, 64% call marriage an important life goal, 47% call it a top priority right now, and 46% say they would like to be married now.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A large latent near-term demand pool exists that current dating infrastructure is failing to convert.
insights.locator: nearly two-thirds (64%) reported that marriage was an important life goal

insights.claim: The temporal disconnect means dating for most young adults is only abstractly associated with marriage — an activity decoupled from the outcome it nominally serves.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Explains why marriage-oriented messaging fails on dating platforms: users are not consciously shopping for spouses.
insights.locator: young adult dating lives are temporally disconnected from marriage expectations

insights.claim: Marriages are significantly more stable today than four to five decades ago, but much of that stability bonus is compositional: riskier-profile couples are simply a shrinking share of those who marry.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Headline divorce-rate improvements are a selection artefact; do not extrapolate them to the whole population.
insights.locator: Granted, much of this stability bonus is a result of who is marrying.

insights.claim: First-marriage rates have fallen by more than 10% over the past two decades and demographers now estimate that a third of young adults born in the early twenty-first century will never marry.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A third never-married cohort reshapes housing demand toward single-occupancy, depresses fertility, and expands the single-person consumption economy.
insights.quote: Demographers now estimate that a third of young adults born in the early decades of the twenty-first century will never marry.
insights.locator: First-marriage rates have fallen by more than 10%

insights.claim: The authors' central metaphor is macroeconomic: the dating system is the on-ramp infrastructure to marriage, and a broken on-ramp produces a 'dating recession' that will depress future marriage rates.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Treats family formation as a market with supply, demand and frictions — a lens that makes dating skills and cost the policy levers rather than values campaigns.
insights.quote: the contemporary dating economy is struggling, perhaps in a recession
insights.locator: If the onramps to our marital highways are bumpy

insights.claim: A healthy majority of young adults still expect a future that includes marriage, though the authors flag this is increasingly less true for young women who lean left ideologically.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Ideological sorting is emerging as a marriage-expectation variable, a leading indicator to watch for further divergence in family formation.
insights.locator: Despite a broken dating system, a healthy majority of young people

insights.claim: The authors identify a 'marital-expectations vs. dating-skills gap' as the defining structural feature of the current cohort.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A single, testable framing that converts a diffuse cultural complaint into a measurable, addressable deficit.
insights.quote: There is a marital-expectations vs. dating-skills gap for most young adults today.
insights.locator: This study shows that there is a marital-expectations

themes.theme: Dating Education as an Unserved Market

insights.claim: Relationship education as an industry serves teens, engaged couples, married couples and couples near divorce, but has left dating education — the on-ramp — essentially unaddressed.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: An identified white space: a service category with documented demand, no incumbents, and adjacent distribution already built.
insights.quote: Generic relationship skills education does not sufficiently address the A-B-C’s of how to date.
insights.locator: Recommendations for Relationship Educators Teaching Dating Skills

insights.claim: The authors predict traditional didactic curricula will fail with this cohort and that digital 'infotainment', peer educators and online delivery will be required to reach them.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Distribution, not content, decides who wins this category — favouring creator-led and platform-native formats over legacy nonprofits.
insights.locator: However, this TikTok generation may not sit still

insights.claim: Because respondents are financially constrained, the authors conclude dating education will have to run as a subsidised public service rather than a for-profit enterprise.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Caps the commercial upside of the category; value accrues to sponsors, foundations and public budgets rather than to venture-scale businesses.
insights.quote: dating education probably will need to be more akin to a public service than a gainful enterprise
insights.locator: One final comment here for dating educators regarding finances

insights.claim: Federal Administration for Children and Families funding currently supports relationship education for couples forming and sustaining marriages but does not permit spending on healthy dating skills education.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A specific, actionable policy gap — a rule change would create the funding base for an entire new service category.
insights.locator: public funds now being allocated by the federal Administration

insights.claim: Structured, skills-infused interventions such as curated speed-dating events are proposed as inertia-breakers whose success is measured by participation and practice rather than by whether couples form.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Redefines the success metric for dating interventions from match rate to activity rate — the same shift the authors argue the market needs.
insights.locator: One colleague we know sponsors carefully constructed speed dating events

insights.claim: The authors insist dating education should not be presented in maritally neutral terms, arguing dating has an inherent purpose that points toward marriage.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A normative stance that will define the ideological split in this emerging category and determine which funders back which providers.
insights.quote: There is a teleology to dating.
insights.locator: it would be wise for relationship educators

insights.claim: The survey did not examine how AI and AI companions are affecting young adult dating lives, an omission the authors explicitly flag as a research gap.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The fastest-moving variable in the youth relationship market is entirely absent from the best current dataset — a blind spot for anyone underwriting AI-companion demand.
insights.quote: we did not explore in our survey how AI and the new world of AI companions may be impacting young adult dating lives
insights.locator: For instance, we did not explore in our survey how AI

insights.claim: The authors concede that perceived low 'marriageability' of men could be shrinking the effective marriage pool and souring dating experiences, even though their survey did not test it directly.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Male labour-force participation and earnings are an untested but plausible upstream driver of the dating recession — worth monitoring alongside the survey metrics.

insights.claim: The growing ideological and political divide between young men and women is named as an unexplored influence on the dating scene.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Political polarisation is being nominated as a family-formation variable; if it bites, it makes the dating recession structurally harder to reverse.
insights.locator: Nor have we explored directly how the growing ideological

insights.claim: The report frames the stakes beyond economics: absent dating experience is a deficit of formative romantic connection, quoting David Brooks that love is the most powerful energy source known to humans.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The moral framing signals how this research will be deployed in policy advocacy, which shapes the political durability of any funding push.
insights.quote: We all need energy sources to power us through life, and love is the most powerful energy source known to humans.
insights.locator: The New York Times columnist David Brooks describes this risk
